newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade independent radio says signal jammed.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade independent radio says signal jammed.

text.p: Journalists at the only independent radio station in the Serbian capital said on Wednesday they suspected authorities were interfering with the station's signal amid the country's biggest street demonstrations in five years.
"We have strong interference and they are trying to jam our transmission," Aleksandar Vasovic, a journalist with Radio B-92, told Reuters.
"It seems to be selective jamming," Vasovic said, "We can be heard in some parts of Belgrade but not in the city centre."
The radio went off the air at least twice and had problems with interference throughout the day, he said.
The station's news editor, Milica Kuburovic, said earlier the station lost its signal at 3:30 p.m. (1430 GMT) for about half an hour, just as opposition protests got under way.
Two other radio stations that shared the same transmitter had no such interference, Kuburovic said.

The timing of the interference -- at the height of opposition protests -- raised concerns among the staff that authorities were trying to clamp down on the city's only radio station outside the control of the ruling Socialist party.
B-92 is the only independent radio station in Belgrade and one of a handful in all of Serbia.
The radio has widely covered a wave of opposition protests demanding President Slobodan Milosevic concede defeat in local elections which the oppposition Zajedno (Together) coalition says it won.
The station has been a thorn in the side of the Socialists in the past, giving a platform to political opponents otherwise completely ignored by the state-controlled television and radio.
Socialists closed the station in 1991, when police occupied its offices and kept it off the air for less than 24 hours.
Authorities have denied B-92 a broadcasting license and have limited the station to a weak signal that cannot be heard beyond Belgrade.
The jamming coincided with reports that authorities were putting pressure on other independent media.

Editors at the new independent daily Blic, which gave the protests front-page coverage, said the state-run printing works had pressed the paper to cut its circulation down from 200,000 to some 80,000 due to "technical difficulties".
Blic journalists said power had been cut to its offices repeatedly over the past couple days.
Late on Wednesday, a group of some 40 Blic reporters said they had walked out of the newspaper offices in protest over a commentary written by one of its owners.
The commentary, which was due to be published on Friday, allegedly "apologised" for the paper's coverage of the street protests, said a reporter who asked not to be named.
The reporters were concerned the paper's owners were caving in to pressure from the authorities.
